nameStory: Fogg's goosefoot gets its species name from a botanist who helped document New England's flora. The "goosefoot" part comes from the shape of the leaves, which reminded early botanists of a goose's webbed foot with its broad, triangular outline and pointed lobes.
description: Fogg's goosefoot is an annual herb that grows as a weedy plant throughout New England. It typically reaches 1-3 feet tall with branching stems and triangular to diamond-shaped leaves. Like other goosefoots, it produces tiny greenish flowers in dense clusters and has a somewhat dusty or mealy appearance on its leaves and stems.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Triangular to diamond-shaped leaves with a distinctive goose-foot outline, often with shallow lobes or teeth along the edges. The leaves feel slightly thick and may have a whitish, powdery coating underneath.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny green flowers without petals, clustered in dense, branching spikes at stem tips and leaf joints. Each flower is barely noticeable individually but creates a greenish, granular appearance in masses.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual herb with branching stems, typically 1-3 feet tall. The plant has a somewhat weedy, informal appearance with multiple branches spreading from the main stem.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, black, lens-shaped seeds that develop where the flowers were. The seeds are shiny and feel smooth when rubbed between fingers, enclosed in papery bracts.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Green to reddish stems that may have faint ridges or grooves running lengthwise. Often with a slightly dusty or mealy texture, especially near the growing tips.

habitat: Fogg's goosefoot grows in disturbed soils, waste areas, and along roadsides throughout New England. It prefers rich, well-drained soils and is often found in agricultural areas, vacant lots, and edges of cultivated fields. This adaptable plant thrives in both sunny and partially shaded locations.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with their characteristic triangular leaves becoming visible. The distinctive leaf shape is already apparent on even small seedlings.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their clusters of tiny green flowers from mid to late summer. This is the best time for identification when both leaves and flowers are present.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and the plant begins to turn yellow-brown, but the distinctive leaf shape remains visible. Seeds are ready to disperse by early fall.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist with dried seed clusters still attached, but the plant dies completely after frost as it's an annual.

funFact: Despite being named for New England botanist John Milton Fogg Jr., this goosefoot is so rare in the region that it has only been documented 7 times - making it one of the most elusive native plants you could possibly encounter on a nature walk!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with Common Lambsquarters, but Fogg's goosefoot tends to have more distinctly triangular leaves with clearer lobing. Remember: if you think you've found Fogg's goosefoot, double-check - it's so rare that it's probably one of its more common cousins instead!
contextualKnowledge: The goosefoot family was recently moved from the Chenopodiaceae family into the larger Amaranth family (Amaranthaceae) based on genetic studies. Many field guides still list goosefoots in their old family, so don't be confused if you see different family names in older references.
compareHints: Fogg's goosefoot is distinguished from Common Lambsquarters by having more triangular, less elongated leaves and typically being smaller overall. Unlike Fig-leaved Goosefoot, its leaves aren't deeply lobed like a fig leaf. The extreme rarity of Fogg's goosefoot in New England means any goosefoot you find is much more likely to be one of the common species in the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common lambsquarters is much more widespread than its relatives like pitseed goosefoot or fig-leaved goosefoot in New England.
Among New England goosefoots, pitseed goosefoot stands out for its strongly toothed lower leaves and honeycomb-pitted seeds.
Unlike common lambsquarters which has simple diamond or triangular leaves, fig-leaved goosefoot has deeply divided, lobed leaves that are unmistakable.

Desert goosefoot stands out from other New England goosefoots primarily by its exceptionally powdery texture - much more pronounced than the light dustiness of common lambsquarters or other relatives.
Tree spinach dwarfs its goosefoot relatives like common lambsquarters, which rarely exceed 3-4 feet tall and have much thinner stems.
Unlike the common lambsquarters with its plain green leaves dusted with white powder, striped goosefoot has those unmistakable light stripes running through each leaf.
